overview: The Zhou rose in present-day Shaanxi and conquered the Shang around 1046 BCE. This imported record begins at 1500 BCE, centuries before that dynasty, and repeats a broad later Western Zhou outline. It cannot show Zhou rule across the whole shaded area throughout. This card separates regional predecessors and late Shang context from early Zhou kingship. The separate Western Zhou and Zhou states cards cover later periods.

periods.title: Regional background in the Shang era
periods.summary: Settlements in the western heartland developed before Zhou dynastic rule. Zaolinhetan was especially active around 1300 to 1100 BCE.

periods.title: A changing western heartland
periods.summary: Zaolinhetan declined as larger centres including Zhouyuan expanded. The archaeological changes do not establish a precise royal founding date.

periods.title: Conquest and early consolidation
periods.summary: Zhou kings replaced Shang royal rule and faced further resistance. The dynasty continued beyond the map cutoff.

sections.title: Before the conquest: homes, food and discovery

items.text: Zaolinhetan in Shaanxi brings small communities into a history often dominated by kings. The 2016 excavation uncovered three houses, rubbish trenches and many pits. Pottery was the largest class of finds, including numerous three-legged li vessels. Ordinary discarded objects help reconstruct life in the Zhou’s western regional background.

Plant and animal evidence at Zaolinhetan points to millet as a staple, with barley and soybeans also present. Pigs, cattle, sheep and goats were among the animals identified. Families depended on crops and animals well before the royal conquest: battles could change rulers without eliminating the need to prepare dinner.

Researchers used 101 radiocarbon dates to test Zaolinhetan’s pottery-based chronology. Much activity fell around 1300 to 1100 BCE, followed by a sharp decline. Different pot shapes sometimes coexisted, so matching a cooking pot to a date or an ethnic group requires more than a quick look at its legs.

In the neighbouring Shang world, rulers asked diviners about illnesses as well as hunts, natural events and warfare. These questions reveal anxiety about health and uncertainty. They record attempts to seek spiritual guidance, rather than clinical evidence that a particular treatment cured disease.

Preparing an oracle bone was skilled work. Bones and turtle shells were cleaned and polished, then grooves and pits were cut into them. A heated rod produced cracks that diviners interpreted. The surviving object combines craftsmanship, ritual and written recordkeeping in one small surface.

Bronze casting began with clay as well as metal. Craftspeople made a model, took a mould in sections, fired those sections and reassembled them around a core. Molten bronze filled the space between them. The core was what kept a magnificent vessel from becoming a useless solid lump.

An early Zhou gui was a grain-serving vessel, often paired with a ding cauldron in ritual. The National Museum’s Li gui has animal-headed handles and a square base. Its practical shape and elaborate decoration turned serving food into a visible statement about its owner and the ancestors being honoured.

A late eleventh-century altar table at the Met accompanies vessels made by different foundries, with several different inscriptions. Curators suggest the group may preserve wealth accumulated in a family shrine. It is a possibility, not a securely excavated household inventory: the reported 1901 tomb discovery lacks a modern excavation record.

Corrosion marks on that altar table preserve outlines left by three vessels. They let researchers partly reconstruct where the vessels stood; the other positions remain hypothetical. An ancient mark on a tabletop can become evidence, even when its original owner might have preferred a spotless surface.

The Kang Hou gui’s inscription recorded a royal honour for future generations as well as living relatives. Food offered in the vessel connected the family with ancestors, while the inscription preserved political achievement. This was memory made durable in bronze, intended to outlast the people who commissioned it.

The Kang Hou gui’s handles are especially lively: horned, tusked animal heads appear to swallow birds, whose beaks poke out. Below them are wings and tails. The same vessel could carry a serious political record and a miniature world of extraordinary creatures.

The Li gui was discovered in 1976 at Xiduan village near Lingkou in Shaanxi. Its inscription recalls the conquest and a subsequent royal gift of metal to Li, who made an ancestral vessel. A reward for service became an object that could preserve both family memory and a major political event.

A short sample from the Li gui is “珷征商”, meaning “Wu campaigned against Shang.” This follows the National Museum’s modern transcription of the bronze inscription; it is not a facsimile of the ancient letter shapes. The museum identifies 珷 as the special form referring to King Wu.

Winning the initial conquest did not end resistance. The eleventh-century Kang Hou gui refers to suppressing a rebellion under King Cheng, after King Wu. Its record connects royal service with establishment in the Wei region. The British Museum specifically distinguishes this episode from the original defeat of Shang.

The early Zhou He zun preserves a king addressing young members of a lineage. They were urged to learn from the service of their fathers, honour ancestors and assist the ruler. This is a specific glimpse of elite instruction and expectations, rather than evidence that every child attended a royal school.

In the same He zun account, the king connected his predecessors’ success with a great heavenly mandate and the duty to govern. He rewarded the recipient with thirty strings of cowries. Moral language, inherited service and valuable gifts helped bind the new political order together.

sections.title: Buildings, work and what later evidence can tell us

items.text: Excavations reported in 2024 identified an early Western Zhou palace wall at Zhouyuan. It lay above earlier pits and was itself cut by early Zhou burials. These overlapping traces establish a sequence of construction and use, giving archaeologists evidence beyond the royal names preserved in texts.

The same project recovered 204 oracle-bone fragments from a ditch beside the palace gate, with a preliminary count of 180 surviving characters. Material apparently discarded from the palace can preserve information that monumental buildings do not. These finds belong to the broader early Western Zhou setting.

Across Zhouyuan’s longer Western Zhou history, excavators have found specialised workshops: bronze casting at Lijia, bone working at Yuntang and jade-ring production at Qijia. These remains reveal organised skilled labour. Their broad dates must not be used to place every workshop before this card’s 1000 BCE cutoff.

Water supply, drainage and roads have also been identified at Zhouyuan. These discoveries show that managing movement and water was part of settlement planning. They are evidence from the wider Western Zhou site, not proof of a toilet in every early household or of one system operating unchanged for centuries.

A study published in 2026 analysed human and animal bones from three Zhouyuan locations. For the broader Western Zhou period, it found a millet-based diet with unequal access to animal protein. This comparison shows why the food celebrated in elite ritual vessels cannot stand for every family’s daily meals.

ending.text: The year 1000 BCE is a division between imported map records, not the fall of Zhou. The dynasty continued; the Western Zhou period lasted until 771 BCE, followed by an eastern court and changing relations with regional states. Communities, crafts and ancestral traditions continued through these political transformations.
